questions.question: 1. What is the worst-case complexity of rebuilding a heap after the root has been replaced?

explanations.a: Correct. Rebuilding or restoring the heap after a root replacement may require moving an element down a path whose length is at most the heap height, which is $O(\log n)$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The root replacement itself can be constant time, but restoring the heap property may require several levels of adjustment.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Restoring a heap after one root replacement does not require processing every element.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single heap restoration is not equivalent to performing a complete heap sort.

questions.question: 2. Does the rebuild operation vary for max and min heaps?

explanations.a: Correct. The restoration logic uses opposite comparison directions: a max-heap keeps larger keys above their children, while a min-heap keeps smaller keys above their children.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Max-heaps and min-heaps use different ordering conditions, so their restoration comparisons are not identical.

questions.question: 3. What is the main purpose of the heapify operation in Heap Sort?

answers.b: To restore the heap property after a change in the heap
answers.d: To search for an element by index

explanations.a: Incorrect. Heapify changes the heap arrangement to satisfy an ordering condition; it does not simply reverse the array.
explanations.b: Correct. Heapify rearranges elements so that the required heap property is restored.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Heapify does not remove duplicate values.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Heapify is a structural adjustment operation, not a search operation.

questions.question: 4. In a max-heap represented as an array, which relationship must hold between a parent and each of its children?

answers.a: Parent is always smaller than both children
answers.b: Parent and children must always be equal
answers.c: Parent is greater than or equal to each child
answers.d: Parent has no ordering relationship with its children

explanations.a: Incorrect. This relationship describes the opposite ordering from the max-heap property.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A heap does not require equal keys among a parent and its children.
explanations.c: Correct. In a max-heap, each parent key is greater than or equal to the keys of its children.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The heap property specifically imposes an ordering relationship between parents and children.

questions.question: 5. Which statement about building a heap from an unsorted array is correct when the bottom-up method is used?

answers.b: It can be done in $O(n)$ time

explanations.a: Incorrect. $O(n\log n)$ is a valid bound for some heap-building approaches, but it is not the tight bound for bottom-up construction.
explanations.b: Correct. Bottom-up heap construction builds a heap from an unsorted array in $O(n)$ time.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Bottom-up heap construction does not require quadratic time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Constructing a heap from an arbitrary array requires work that grows with the number of elements.

questions.question: 6. During Heap Sort with a max-heap, why is the root exchanged with the last element of the unsorted portion?

answers.a: To place the current maximum in its final sorted position
answers.b: To make the root the minimum element

explanations.a: Correct. The root contains the maximum element, so exchanging it with the last unsorted position places that element where it belongs in ascending order.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The exchange does not change the max-heap into a min-heap.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The exchange removes one position from the active heap rather than increasing its size.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The exchange is followed by restoring the heap property when necessary.

questions.question: 7. What is the space complexity of an in-place implementation of Heap Sort, excluding the input array?

explanations.a: Incorrect. An in-place implementation does not require a separate array proportional to $n$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The sorting process does not allocate $O(n\log n)$ additional storage.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Although the heap has logarithmic height, the standard in-place Heap Sort does not need $O(\log n)$ auxiliary storage for the iterative heap operations.
explanations.d: Correct. In-place Heap Sort uses $O(1)$ auxiliary space when the implementation uses iterative heap adjustments.

questions.question: 8. Which sequence of steps best describes Heap Sort using a max-heap for ascending order?

answers.a: Build a max-heap, repeatedly move the root to the end of the unsorted portion, reduce the heap size, and restore the heap property
answers.b: Build a min-heap and repeatedly move the root to the beginning without restoring the heap
answers.c: Repeatedly find the minimum by scanning the entire array and place it at the end
answers.d: Build a max-heap once and leave the array unchanged after construction

explanations.a: Correct. These steps describe the standard in-place Heap Sort process for producing ascending order.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This sequence does not describe the standard max-heap-based procedure for ascending Heap Sort.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Repeated full-array scans describe a different selection-based approach rather than Heap Sort.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Building the heap is only the initial phase; further extraction and restoration steps are required to sort the array.

questions.question: 9. Why does Heap Sort have $O(n\log n)$ worst-case time complexity?

answers.a: Because each of the $n$ elements is compared with every other element
answers.c: Because each extraction can require $O(\log n)$ adjustment and this is repeated for the elements
answers.d: Because the array is divided into two equal parts at every step

explanations.a: Incorrect. Comparing every pair of elements would lead to a quadratic number of comparisons.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The bottom-up construction of the heap is not quadratic.
explanations.c: Correct. Heap Sort performs a linear number of extraction steps, and each heap restoration can take $O(\log n)$, resulting in $O(n\log n)$ worst-case time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Heap Sort does not use recursive halving in the way merge-based algorithms do.
